extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning proofs and basic set theory / cardinality
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition, proof, and worked examples showing how to use injections f:A→B and g:B→A to produce a bijection h:A→B (the Cantor–Bernstein–Schroeder theorem), plus related examples and exercises about cardinalities of intervals, R, and power sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor–Bernstein criterion for equal cardinality
rubrics_metrics.description: If |A| ≤ |B| and |B| ≤ |A| (i.e., there are injections f:A→B and g:B→A), then |A| = |B|; equivalently, given injections f:A→B and g:B→A one can produce a bijection h:A→B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the main theorem: when proving two sets have equal cardinality it suffices to exhibit injections in both directions and then apply the Cantor–Bernstein–Schroeder theorem to conclude existence of a bijection (possibly constructed explicitly as in the proof).

rubrics_metrics.name: Partition-of-A construction (define G and W)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define G = ⋃_{k≥0} (g∘f)^k (A − g(B)) ⊆ A and W = A − G, partitioning A into 'gray' (G) and 'white' (W) regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof constructs the subset G (elements that arise from iterating g∘f starting from A−g(B)) and its complement W; this partition is essential to define the bijection h piecewise. Explain and justify why this union indeed partitions A and characterize elements of G by their position in the alternating chain B→A→B→A→···.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the bijection h piecewise
rubrics_metrics.description: Define h:A→B by h(x)=f(x) for x∈G and h(x)=g^{-1}(x) for x∈W (note g^{-1} denotes the inverse g: B→g(B) restricted and inverted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make sure g^{-1}(x) is defined for x∈W (i.e., W⊆g(B)), and that f maps G into B. This piecewise definition is the explicit bijection built from the two injections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of inverse on g(B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although g:B→A may not be surjective onto A, the restriction g:B→g(B) is a bijection and therefore has an inverse g^{-1}: g(B)→B which may be used in the construction of h on W.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly observe and justify that g:B→g(B) is bijective so the inverse g^{-1} is well-defined on g(B). Show W⊆g(B) so g^{-1} applies to all x∈W.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injectivity proof by exhaustive cases
rubrics_metrics.description: To show h is injective consider three cases: (i) x,y∈G, (ii) x,y∈W, (iii) one in G and one in W; use injectivity of f and of g and properties of G to rule out or resolve each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For (i) use f injective; for (ii) apply g to both sides and use g injective; for (iii) show impossibility via the definition of G (an element described as (g∘f)^k(z) for z∈A−g(B)). Present each case clearly and use the structure of G to derive a contradiction in the mixed-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surjectivity proof by element chasing in the chain
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove h is surjective, take arbitrary b∈B and examine g(b)∈A: if g(b)∈W then h(g(b))=b; if g(b)∈G then express g(b)=(g∘f)^k(z) for some z∈A−g(B) and k>0, find x=(g∘f)^{k−1}(z)∈G so that h(x)=f(x)=b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The surjectivity argument relies on following the alternating chain and using the definitions of G and h to produce a preimage for any b∈B. Carefully justify k>0 in the relevant case and use injectivity of g when deducing intermediate equalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical strategy: prefer injections when bijections are hard
rubrics_metrics.description: When trying to show two sets have the same cardinality, it is often easier to find injections both ways and then apply Cantor–Bernstein rather than attempting to write down an explicit bijection directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The textbook emphasizes that 'injections are often easier to find than bijections' and demonstrates how the theorem turns two injections into a bijection; use this strategy for sets like intervals or infinite sets where bijections can be awkward to construct directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of injections via decimal/encoding representations
rubrics_metrics.description: To map [0,1) into A(ℕ) use the unique decimal expansion 0.b1b2b3… (excluding expansions that end in repeating 9's) and send 0.b1b2… to the set {10^{b1}, 10^{b2}, …} (an injective encoding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure decimal representations are unique by disallowing trailing 9's (e.g., the convention that decimals do not end with an infinite tail of 9s). Use digit-based encodings to create injections from real-intervals to sets of natural-number-indexed objects; explain injectivity by finding the first digit index where two numbers differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of injections from power sets to intervals via characteristic-decimals
rubrics_metrics.description: Define g:A(ℕ)→[0,1) by mapping a subset X⊆ℕ to the decimal 0.b1b2b3… where bi=1 if i∈X and bi=0 otherwise; this map is injective because different sets differ at some index.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When encoding subsets as decimals, show injectivity by exhibiting the smallest index where two characteristic sequences differ and observing the corresponding decimal digits differ, hence the reals differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care with uniqueness and conventions in decimal-based constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: When using decimal expansions to encode or decode sets/numbers be explicit about the uniqueness convention (e.g., exclude representations with repeating trailing 9's) to avoid ambiguity in mappings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the convention clearly and verify it is used in injectivity arguments (so that each real in [0,1) has a unique expansion for the encoding/decoding to be well-defined and injective).
